analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in 1596. United States against Morrow and Fusco. Mr. Kye, I think you may proceed now. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court, this case is also here to review a judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. In this case, affirming an order of the District Court dismissing criminal contempt prosecutions against the two respondents herein on the ground that Article 4E of the Interstate Agreement on detainers had been violated when these federal defendants were returned to state prison between arraignment and trial. I have a lot of ground that I'd like to cover, and I think the facts essentially are very simple and can be stated very briefly. The criminal contempt indictments were returned at a time when both Morrow and Fusco were prisoners in New York State prisons. They were returned in the Eastern District of New York, in the same state, in other words. A writ of habeas corpus ad prosequindum was issued. No detainer was ever lodged against them on this criminal contempt charge. And they were brought into federal court. They pleaded not guilty. Their trial was scheduled. There was some discussion about whether they would stay in the Metropolitan Correctional Center, which is a federal pretrial detention facility in New York. Fusco indicated that he wanted to be returned to state prison. Morrow, that he wished to stay in the federal holding facility. In fact, the federal holding facility was overcrowded, and both of them were returned to state prison. Subsequently, well, the record doesn't show. Subsequently, their lawyer, in what I think is a stroke of genius, made the motion to dismiss under the interstate agreement of detainers and prevailed. The Court of Appeals, in a two-to-one decision, upheld that action, concluding that if the writ of habeas corpus ad prosequindum were not treated as both a detainer and a request, the effect would be to allow the federal government to circumvent the requirements of the interstate agreement on detainers by not filing, not lodging a detainer against the prisoner. Now, I'd like to discuss first the general considerations, which I believe are the same in this case as in the prior case, for why the writ should not be construed to constitute either a detainer or a request. The interstate agreement on detainers affected a dramatic change in the way state prosecutors could procure out-of-state prisoners for trial, and it provided for them a needed mechanism to deal with a very real problem in the case of state-to-state transfers, and with federal adherence to the agreement to deal with a real problem securing federal prisoners for state trial. It gave federal prosecutors, however, nothing that they did not, as a realistic matter, fully enjoy before federal adherence to the agreement. There may have been an occasional instance in which a federal ad prosecutum writ was not honored. I think in the Ford case, a respondent's attorney found maybe two cases where that occurred. It simply was not a realistic practical problem, and it was not on anybody's mind. Are we to assume that when it was not honored, the federal government just dropped the matter? That's apparently what happened because... In the Gordon case, it was about two witnesses. It wasn't a defendant. Well, I think they were co-defendants. They were also wanted as witnesses. And the statement that they use is dictum about five lines below. The issue arises in cases where the defendant is subsequently claiming that he should have been produced and his speedy trial rights were violated or that the witnesses, his co-defendant, should have been produced, and the court observes and then cites the Ponzi case for the proposition that compliance is a matter of comedy. We're fully prepared to stand on the proposition that the Supremacy Clause would compel requirement in the event that there were a federal-state confrontation, which is not to say that the state warden couldn't come into federal court under an analogy to the abstention doctrine and say, for instance, we're in the middle of a state trial, would you stay with all the... We don't have to decide that question here. Absolutely not. It's only pertinent in terms of understanding whether there was a problem that was dealt with by the interstate agreement on detainers, and we maintain that there was absolutely no problem with federal prosecutors getting state prisoners for trial. That was the concern of either the Council of State Governments or the Congress. On this issue, you agree with Judge Mansfield? On the issue that the... Whether or not this is a detainer. Whether or not this is a detainer. But when you say this issue, I'm addressing the broader issue first, because if we win on the issue of whether the writ is a request, we win this case. We can also win this case, even if the writ is a request, on the grounds that the writ is not a detainer. And the arguments as to why the writ is not a detainer are, I think, fairly clear and have been well canvassed in our brief and in Judge Mansfield's dissenting opinion. And I hope to address myself principally to the legislative history of the Speedy Trial Act and the other factors that we think compel the conclusion that it's not even a request, let alone a detainer. The things that our questions prevented you from addressing yourself to in the first argument. Perhaps, but they are fully relevant to this case. Now, in focusing on what the problem was that prompted the Council of State Governments to adopt a provision such as Article 4, I think it's crystal clear that they were not talking about the federal procedure with the ad prosequindum writ. And I'd like to quote just a sentence from the statement of the Council of State Governments in connection with the circulation of the agreement as a proposal that they were recommending. They state, In addition, the only way that a prosecuting official can secure for trial a person already imprisoned in another jurisdiction is by resort to a cumbersome special contract with the executive authority of the incarcerating state. Because of the difficulty in red tape involved in securing such contracts, they are little used. Well, that's obviously not a description of the federal experience in procuring state prisoners. If the states had the same right, they wouldn't need the bill at all. If the states had a habeas corpus writ that ran outside their boundaries, that's true. Well, there would still be problems about how to handle expenses, about... One of the great concerns, one of the reasons the sending state was reluctant to relinquish a prisoner was they wanted an assurance that they would get him back after the trial in the receiving state. Now, Congress enacted the interstate agreement as federal law in 1970. I think it's unmistakably clear to anybody who reads the legislative history that the motivation underlying federal adoption of the agreement was for two purposes and two purposes only. The first was to facilitate the efforts of states to procure federal prisoners for trial and to supply for federal prisoners a mechanism for clearing state detainers. This was thought particularly pressing in light of the decision a year earlier in Smith against Huy involving the speedy trial obligations of states with respect to federal prisoners. The second objective was to provide a means for the District of Columbia to procure state prisoners for trial. Now, it's impossible to believe that Congress meant to alter the means whereby the federal government acquired state prisoners for trial and to impose new conditions such as the no return and the speedy trial requirements of Article 4 in connection with those proceedings. There's no mention of any such consequence in the section discussing the need for the legislation, and it seems at least passing strange that if Congress envisioned this consequence for federal prosecutions, it's discussion of this aspect of the agreement was confined to the effect on the District of Columbia. And, of course, the statement by the Commissioner of the District of Columbia, or the Assistant Commissioner, which was not echoed by the Deputy Attorney General's explanation of what the bill would accomplish, I think should be given very little weight. Moreover, a review of the various provisions of the agreement reflects anomalies that surely would have been addressed had Congress realized that it was changing the procedures whereby the federal government obtains the presence of state prisoners for trial. The agreement is set forth in the appendix to our brief in Ford. The most obvious provision, which has been much discussed, is the proviso to Article 4A, which is at page 8A of the appendix, which gives the governor 30 days to disapprove the request. Now, I'm sure that Congress thought that when a state prisoner was wanted for federal trial, the governor had no power to say, no, we won't deliver him any more than the southern governors had power after Browning and Board of Education to interpose state sovereignty to resist federal orders there. And I think it would be extraordinary for Congress to create such a power in state governors, which they surely must not have thought previously existed without saying a word about it. Indeed, whatever problems there may have been with the occasional case prior to federal adherence to the agreement where some state warden refused to honor the writ, these problems would surely be multiplied if this proviso in the agreement applied. Now, secondly, Article 4C of the agreement is significant because it refers to, in respect of any proceeding made possible by this article, that's the speedy trial provision. Now, the notion that underlies this is that Article 4 was making possible certain proceedings that were not previously possible or feasible, that it was providing... Mr. Brian, on that point, I must say I think you're probably arguing the Ford case more than the Morrill case now, but that's all right. On that very point, supposing Indiana and Illinois, prior to the adoption of this agreement, had worked out an informal procedure where they exchanged prisoners upon request and worked out the finances and all the rest, so that they never had a problem. Would this article apply to them after they both signed the agreement? Not if they continued to use the prior procedures. Not if they didn't file this... Not if they didn't procure prisoners by filing this request for temporary. I think they have to use that particular form or else the agreement wouldn't... That form or some other statement invoking the rights under Article 4 of the agreement. So that your construction is that the agreement only applies to those states which could demonstrate that they had previously been having problems getting prisoners. Well, the agreement applies... Even those states, I think, by and large abandoned their resort to executive contract. Even if they used the agreement form, your argument would still apply, because if they hadn't been having difficulties before, the procedure wouldn't have been made possible by the agreement. But I think what that language means is that when you have... What the framers had in mind was that this agreement was providing a mechanism that did not previously exist that was different from ones that previously existed. There was, after all, extradition, which the states could still resort to. There were these special contracts, which the state would still resort to. No, but your very technical reading of the language is that the criminal trial has to have been made possible. Isn't that right? No, I don't think so. I think that is talking about a proceeding to receive the prisoner from one state to another. I see. But you would say that if there were a preexisting procedure... Well, I'm not quite clear on your argument. I would say that if there were a preexisting procedure... I don't think what they mean by this is that the agreement applies only when it was impossible previously to get a prisoner from one state to another because it wasn't impossible previously. It was just extremely difficult. I think what they mean by this is when you avail yourself of the mechanism which we have supplied you here, then you've got to... There are certain costs that are associated with certain responsibilities that we're going to impose on you. One is the speedy trial obligation. The second is the no return obligation. These are a quid pro quo for a very substantial benefit that state prosecutors were getting, and I think that's what that... So, in other words, you've made it as Zoya just said. In respect of any proceeding under this article, basically, that's the way you interpret it. Well, I think it means more than that for us because if that was all it said, it wouldn't help me at all because that would not get around the question. I think what it means is any proceeding that is facilitated by this article. Now, I don't think they had in mind the situation that Indiana and Illinois were going along swimmingly before, and really they didn't get any advantage out of this, but still for some reason they used this form and made a request under this agreement. I think if a request was made under this agreement and custody was delivered in accordance with the terms of this agreement, then the consequence would be that the conditions related there to it. Well, then it all comes back to the question whether the writ is a request under the terms of the agreement. It's still the same basic argument, same basic issue. Well, but I don't think that the speedy trial provision, literally read, can apply on... I think it's clear that the meaning of that provision is that your procurement of the prisoner has to have been facilitated. I don't think it makes any sense to say that this procedure was... But you say that in the state-federal context, but then you say you don't make that argument as between two states that were getting along swimmingly. Oh, I would make that... I would make the same argument if Illinois procured a prisoner from Indiana under their old procedures, and then the court set over the... And it signed this agreement and then kept the man for 130 days, you'd say he had no right under this agreement. I would say if the defendant said, well, you should treat this old procedure as a request under this agreement in order to prevent them from circumventing the agreement, I would say that I would disagree with that argument. If Illinois, in the same... asked for him under four, and Indiana said we'll give him to you under the old rule... Well, I think then... Would you think that that's... I'm not sure. I mean, there are a lot of combinations that can be played on this. What I'm trying to get at is who controls the destiny of this prisoner, the receiving state or the delivering state? The receiving state has the right under the agreement or under other procedures that may exist to secure... You would have the right under either. Probably under either. We might have the right under the interstate agreement on detainers if we wanted to invoke it. Could a couple of states enter into a side agreement saying we will only use the agreement on the detainers when we really need to? Our general practice shall be the old-fashioned one where you give it to us and we'll take it and we'll let the detainers still have all the adverse consequences it used to have. There'll be no speedy trial rights, all the rest. We'll just stay outside the agreement. Would that be permitted? Well, it would be permitted with respect to Article 4. There would be no problem. The evils of the detainers were really addressed in Article 3. And if the states were adherents to the agreement, the prisoner would have a right to demand a trial under Article 3. But what we're talking about here is Article 4. And that is not addressed to the evils of the detainer system at all, but to the difficulty of the state prosecutor obtaining a prisoner from another state for trial. So that I don't think there would be any problem in saying if the states wanted to not take advantage of what Article 4 had given to them, they also wouldn't have to pay the price that's associated with using Article 4. And we haven't taken advantage of Article 4. But isn't the 120-day speedy trial requirement for the benefit of the prisoner, not for the demanding state? Well, it is for the benefit of the prisoner in the sense that once you start the proceedings, you're obliged to continue them. But what I'm suggesting is that Article 4 basically was put in there to help the state prosecutor. But as a condition of rendering this assistance to the state prosecutor, which he desperately needed, certain conditions were imposed. If you're going to do this, you're going to have to comply with the 120-day requirement and so on. Well, what if the, I'm not saying it normally happens, but what if the prosecutor says, somebody comes in and says, look, you know you're just grabbing this guy because we can't try him within 120 days. And the prosecutor says, well, take back that Article 4 thing and let's go by hebe. I would be wrong. I suppose if he once used it, he would be, well. You and I can't conceive of a prosecutor doing that. No, but I'm not sure. I don't think once he started the ball rolling under the agreement, I don't think he could stop it. For any reason. Well, except for continuance in open court for good cause and so on. Now, the conclusion that nobody understood federal adherence to the detainer agreement to alter the traditional use of the writ is confirmed by the events that followed its enactment. Although the speedy trial and no return provisions would obviously constitute dangerous booby traps for the unwary federal prosecutor, as Mr. Justice Stewart suggested earlier, if federal procurement of state prisoners was to be regulated by Article 4, the Justice Department, which had sponsored this legislation in Congress, breathed not a word of these dire consequences to federal prosecutors. Instead, it assigned the responsibility for administering federal participation in the agreement to the Bureau of Prisons, which was intimately involved with the responsibilities as a sending state, but had at most a tangential connection when the United States is a receiving state. Mr. Fry, do you think that federal courts could ignore the dire consequences of the Speedy Trial Act on the ground that Congress didn't know what it was doing when it asked federal judges to handle all these cases without having enough federal judges to do the work? No. Because Congress obviously didn't know the consequences of that statute. But the question here is whether these are consequences. I would agree that if Article 4A said any proceeding instituted by the writ of habeas corpus ad prosequendum by a federal prosecutor shall be subject to the following conditions, then regardless of how little considered it was or what the consequences were, the courts would be obliged to follow it. But it certainly is a basic tenet of statutory construction that in deciding how to deal with ambiguous or even in training against Colorado public interest research group with what seemed to be very clear, language, the court can consider the absurdities that might be created, the extent to which it defeats the congressional purposes, and the extent to which it creates problems with other legislation. And in this connection, the Second Circuit made no mention of the Speedy Trial Act, but I think it's very important to judicial consideration of this statute. The Speedy Trial Act was adopted by Congress only four years after it had adopted the Detainer Agreement, and in adopting it, Congress reflected not the slightest awareness that it had already legislated on the question of trial deadlines and procedures for state prisoners brought in for federal trial. The result is a scheme that is at best redundant with the Speedy Trial protections that the Court of Appeals found already existed under the agreement and is in several respects inconsistent with them. Wasn't there some opposition to the enactment of the Speedy Trial Act? Yes. The Speedy Trial Act was a much considered, in contrast to the interstate agreement on detainers, it was considered in quite some detail, and the Department, the Justice Department, had some opposition to some of its provisions and structure. Was the judicial conference the United States involved? I am not sure. I think it may well have been. Yes, it's a matter of public record that they, by unanimous votes, the judicial conference opposed the passage of the Act. Well, I know. But no hearings were conducted of any significance to let that opposition be heard. Did any of the opponents to the enactment of the legislation mention in any way the existence of the interstate detainer? I'm not aware of it. If they did, it did escape my attention. I mean, I think nobody mentioned it because it's quite clear that nobody thought it applied. Well, you were asleep at the switch, as I said earlier. That may be, but I think that in terms of what Congress thought, in terms of what the Department of Justice thought, in terms of what the courts thought, in terms of what the defense bar thought, nobody thought it applied. Everybody thought when the government proceeded by the ad prosecutum writ, it was doing what it had always done. Well, that's true. That much is true. That didn't get you very far in the argument. Well, I think it gets me quite away because I think that it shows that there is no reason why this court should go out of its way to say that a request, under Article 4A of the agreement, that a writ of habeas corpus ad prosequendum is a request. There's nothing, I mean, there's no linguistic equivalence in those two terms. The writ on its face is a command. Now, it's true that you could say a command is a kind of request, but this is an area in which the court has full flexibility to do what seems appropriate to achieve the congressional purposes and to produce a harmonious and rational scheme of legislation. And the problems, if you rule against us in the speedy trial area, there are serious problems of inconsistencies that will bedevil the courts in the future. And to take one example, the tolling provisions for extending the time beyond, and under the interstate agreement on detainers, you have 120 days. Any extension thereafter must be for good cause shown, and it has to be in open court with the defendant or his counsel present. Now, on the other hand, under the Speedy Trial Act, you have 60 days. There are tolling provisions, however, so that if in the middle of those 60 days there's a competency inquiry, there's an interlocutory appeal by the government, some other event, those days simply don't count, which is quite different from the interstate agreement. What's more, continuances can be granted under the Speedy Trial Act. They don't have to be in open court. The defendant or his counsel does not have to be present. But on the other hand, there does have to be a statement of reasons on the record, either oral or written. Now, we're asking for... Well, I suppose if you lose prosecutors in courts, we'll just have to abide by the highest common denominator of the two overlapping statutes. Well, there are going to be a lot of mistakes which will accomplish no substantial protection of anybody's rights, but an awful lot of litigation for the courts. Well, people say that about the Speedy Trial Act generally. Well... But Congress enacted it. Mr. Fry, are you going to argue the moral case? Oh, yes. First of all, every one of these arguments is... If you win on that argument, you win the moral case, too, but you're kind of putting all your eggs in one basket. Because the issue in the moral case, as I understand, is whether the writ is a detainer, not whether the writ is a request. Of course, our contention that the writ is not a request... If you win on the first point, in the other case, you win both cases. I agree with that. But you're not going to argue the moral case separately, because you have really quite a strong argument in the moral case. Oh, I have a very strong argument, and as I indicated earlier to Mr. Justice Stewart, I had intended to rely largely on Judge Mansfield's dissent. I mean, I think it is clear that whatever else was intended, the framers of the agreement and Congress were dealing with the problems that are created by the lodging of a detainer, and I think it is clear that the writ ad prosequendum is not a detainer. It functions in a different way, and there's no reason to do... May I ask this, Mr. Fry. You asked me to emphasize the practical situation. There's some 5,000 people. Is it each year there are 5,000 writs issued, or is that over 3,000? That is the information that we have from the Marshal Service. That doesn't mean 5,000 different people, because the writ could be issued more than once with respect to the same... First for indictment, then for trial. First for arraignment, then for motions. Am I correct that about 3,000 of those are cases where there were a detainer, and the other 2,000 is no detainer? That's our information. So the 2,000 would be solved if you win the moral case. Now, as to the 3,000, supposing this issue could not be raised on collateral attack, and that's something we don't have here, is it not true that that would solve a great many of those that are outstanding now? Well, that would solve many of the past cases, but I'm... Wouldn't it minimize the overwhelming character of this problem? Well, it would minimize the problem, but it would by no means eliminate it, because there are not only the inconsistencies with the speedy trial act that I've just mentioned, but there are even worse problems with the no return provision. The no return provision... First of all, something... Couldn't you solve the no return problem by just asking the prisoner if he wants to go back or not? Well... And usually, as I understand it, when you've pulled him out, you've got him in a very temporary, undesirable facility. So wouldn't he normally want to go back to the more permanent... Well, he might or might not want to go back. I understand... Well, if you're aware of the problem, you give him the option, what's the difficulty? The problem could be... Just give him the choice. The problem could be solved. I'm not saying that in the normal case... It isn't a very simple problem. Extraordinarily simple problem. It's not extraordinarily simple, because if you look at a case like Thompson, the Third Circuit case, which we have a pending petition for certiorari in, Thompson was in the state jail, which happened to be also the facility where federal prisoners are held. A detainer had been lodged against him, and he was then indicted on heroin distribution charges and brought in by writ into the federal court to plead, returned several hours later to the same jail that he came from, which also was the jail where he would have been kept as a federal prisoner. But the paperwork that would have transformed him from a state prisoner into a federal prisoner wasn't done. And what we're going to have to rely on is that the secretaries in the marshal's office don't make a mistake with their paperwork, because if they do, a defendant is going to get a windfall dismissal. As you say, this was during the period when this was kind of a time bomb ticking away, and nobody realized it was there. But once you know the problem, can't you handle the paperwork? The problem is, yes, it can be done, but I'm saying that mistakes are made. We know what Rule 11 requires district judges to do in the course of accepting a guilty plea, but I can assure you that across my desk come dozens of cases in which they don't do it. Now, we should repeal Rule 11 because judges don't follow it? No, I'm not suggesting. We ban this agreement because people are going to make mistakes and not be able to follow it? I don't understand this kind of legal argument. I'm simply suggesting that you should not assume. I'm not asking you to do anything affirmative on that ground so much as asking that you not assume that there will be no problem in the future as an empirical matter if you make it clear that the agreement applies, because, in fact, there will be problems. But, Mr. Fry, isn't it a fact that this whole statute was adopted because there was a very serious problem of people subject to detainers being subjected to unfair treatment? Isn't that to be weighed in the scale? That is... And the government, I think, agrees with that. There is no evidence, Mr. Justice Stevens, that there was any concern on the part of Congress or, indeed, on the part of the Council of State Governments with the effect of federal detainers. There's simply no... They were not addressed... But doesn't the evidence indicate that about half the detainers were issued by the federal government? That's true, and yet it's clear from the focus of the discussions that it was on the effect of state detainers. And let me make another point, because the Speedy Trial Act now provides a mechanism for the state prisoner to clear the federal detainer. So we're back in the situation where we don't need two mechanisms. We don't need both the agreement and the Speedy Trial Act. He can do it under the Speedy Trial Act. In fact, Congress dealt with the problem there consciously, which I don't believe anybody could conclude it did in this area. And I think, just to sum up, that if the Court holds that the provisions of Article 4 of the Interstate Agreement are inapplicable when the federal government uses the RID. This holding would not undermine the expectations or goals of Congress. It would not subvert the concerns that led the Council of State Governments to adopt the agreement, but rather it would create a harmonious relationship between the habeas corpus statute, the Speedy Trial Act, and the Interstate Agreement on Detainers. The state prisoner with a federal detainer can clear the detainer under the Speedy Trial Act. The state prosecutor who wants a federal prisoner can resort to the agreement, and Speedy Trials are guaranteed under the Speedy Trial Act. Now, I can't see why the Court should go out of its way to construe the writ as a request to undermine this essentially symmetrical system which provides adequate protection for all of the defendant's interests and the interests of the criminal justice system. I'll save it all, Mr. Pryor. Mr. Ross. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court. I would like to stress at first a few facts with regards to the Morrow case that I believe were not covered sufficiently. First thing is this. Mr. Morrow and Mr. Fusco were prisoners in the Auburn Correctional Facility in Auburn, New York. At the time of their indictment in the Eastern District of New York. Now, Auburn, New York is approximately 300 miles from Brooklyn. After their indictment in the beginning of November 1975, they were produced in Brooklyn by writ. They were arraigned on November 24th, and they again appeared on December 2nd in court. They were returned, however, on both December 11th, I believe, and December 19th back to Auburn. Now, the reason why I stress these facts is that this is not a case in which a prisoner is produced on writ for the purpose of one discreet appearance in court and then returned the same day to his place of incarceration so that he has no substantial damage to his prospects of rehabilitation or treatment. This is a case in which there was a clear abuse of the purposes of the agreement. Now, the reason why I say this is that the Second Circuit has recently decided a case in which precisely this issue was before the court. The name of the case was United States against Chico. I'm sorry it wasn't in my brief, but it was reported after our briefs were filed. Now, in that case, Judge Mansfield... Do you have a citation there? Yes, I do, Your Honor. It's 558 F21047. Now, in that case, interestingly enough, Judge Mansfield wrote the decision, and in that case there was the production of a prisoner on writ in the District of Connecticut, and he was returned the same day to his place of incarceration. Now, Judge Mansfield, writing for unanimous bench, held that under these circumstances, there has not been the change in the conditions of confinement which would warrant the enforcement of the interstate agreement on detainers. From this case, I believe I see a coherent scheme in the interpretation of the agreement. And that is this. We do not look at the document which causes the transfer of the prisoner. We look at the transfer of the prisoner. For example, in the Morrow case, we have a case in which the prisoners were shuttled back and forth over a matter of months. They remained in Manhattan for three or four weeks at a time. For this reason, I don't think it would matter that the document itself that causes the transfer of the prisoner is called a writ instead of a detainer. Now, the government attempts in its brief to distinguish the writ from the detainer by stating that the writ is immediately executed, and therefore it doesn't have the long-term perspective effects or future damaging effects of a detainer. However, I believe that the same analysis applies to that argument. The writ itself, although immediately executed, causes a complete disjunction, I'm sorry, a complete fragmentation of the continuity of rehabilitation, so that the prisoner is shuttled from one jurisdiction to another. What do you think the word detainer in the statute means? Of course, this is one of the main issues of the case, Your Honor.
